card.hook: Every building around Piazza Maggiore looks like it's trying to get into your photo, and honestly, they all deserve to. The best view is from above, looking down on a sea of red rooftops.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top of the Torre dell'Orologio, the clock tower inside Palazzo d'Accursio on the Piazza Maggiore side. Face east: the square lies to the east of you, ringed by San Petronio and the palaces.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the square and the buildings around it. Tap 0.5x to squeeze the whole square into one frame, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out San Petronio or the distant towers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the square, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the rooftops keep their colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the rooftops best. Check the tower's opening times before you plan your visit.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Fountain of Neptune in Piazza del Nettuno, the small plaza right next to the main square, and try a selfie beside the bronze fountain. Use the front camera at 1x, or 0.5x if you want more of the buildings over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Out on the open square, face San Petronio's unfinished façade and ask someone to take a wide shot of you with the basilica behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the public areas of the square, but churches and museums may have their own rules on signs. The tower is a ticketed visit and access can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Spot San Petronio's unfinished façade and get it in your frame, then see if you can fit Neptune and his fountain in a second shot.
card.good_to_know: Piazza Maggiore has been Bologna's central meeting place since medieval times. Palazzo d'Accursio, on the west side, is the city hall and a museum. San Petronio is the city's Duomo, and its unfinished façade is one of the easiest things to recognise in a photo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top of the Torre dell'Orologio, the clock tower inside Palazzo d'Accursio on the Piazza Maggiore side. Face east: the square lies to the east of you, ringed by San Petronio and the palaces.

card.hook: Walk east along Via Rizzoli and the street ends with two leaning brick towers waiting for you, like a postcard that learned to stand up. This is the angle on most of the postcards, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Stand on Via Rizzoli, under the portico, and face east along the straight street toward the towers at the far end. Both should rise ahead of you, with the Garisenda's lean showing against the sky.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x with your phone held upright, so you fit the Asinelli's full height and the Garisenda's lean in one shot. Switch to 1x for a tighter, cleaner view of the pair, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details like the top of the Asinelli.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky near the towers, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the brickwork stays visible.
card.best_time: Early morning or evening, when the light is soft. If the light fades in the evening, try night mode with your phone braced against a pillar of the portico.
card.selfie_here: Head to Piazza di Porta Ravegnana, the small square at the foot of the towers, and stand with the leaning towers behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Via Rizzoli, a short distance back from the towers, while you stand at the base of the towers so both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The Garisenda has been sealed off since October 2023 while work to stabilise it goes on, so you can only photograph it from outside. The Asinelli may or may not be open, so check on the day with Bologna Welcome or the comune.
card.challenge: Can you get the Garisenda's lean in your shot with no fences or lampposts poking in, and a portico arch framing one edge?
card.good_to_know: The towers are traditionally credited to two local families and dated to between 1109 and 1119, though few documents survive to confirm it. The Asinelli stands about 97 metres tall, while the Garisenda is only about 48 metres but leans by around 3.2 metres. It was once much taller and was shortened in the 14th century when the ground beneath it gave way. Dante mentions it in his writing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Via Rizzoli, under the portico, and face east along the straight street toward the towers at the far end. Both should rise ahead of you, with the Garisenda's lean showing against the sky.

card.hook: Picture a giant church wearing a smart marble jacket on the bottom half and going without on top. That's San Petronio, and the bare red brick is the whole charm. Work began in 1390 and the front was never finished.
card.stand_here: Stand out on Piazza Maggiore, the open square on the church's north side, and face the basilica, which fills the south side of the square. Leave some open square at the bottom of your shot so you can see how big the building is.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole façade across the square. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the palaces around it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carvings on the main doorway and the line where marble meets brick.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap the façade and drag the brightness slider a touch darker so the pale marble keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go before about 9 a.m. for a quieter square and softer light, so you can get a clean frame without crowds in front of the doors. Sunrise or sunset adds a warm glow to the façade.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Piazza Maggiore, on the open square facing the marble-and-brick front, with the façade behind you. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone has it on the front) and tilt up a little so the church fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square near the Palazzo del Podestà, directly across from the basilica, while you stand in front of the façade and they frame you with the whole front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is discouraged at the basilica, and it's a good idea to keep bags and strollers out of the walkways while you take your photos.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 2x and find the exact spot where the marble gives up and the bare brick begins, then snap it and see if your friends can guess where it is.
card.good_to_know: The basilica is dedicated to Bologna's patron saint, Saint Petronius, who was Bishop of Bologna in the fifth century. It's huge: about 132 metres long, 66 metres wide and 47 metres tall. The main doorway, the Porta Magna, has carved scenes and figures by Jacopo della Quercia.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out on Piazza Maggiore, the open square on the church's north side, and face the basilica, which fills the south side of the square. Leave some open square at the bottom of your shot so you can see how big the building is.

card.hook: You've climbed a very long hill, your legs are complaining, and then Bologna rolls out below you like a terracotta carpet. That view is your reward, so take a few photos before you sit down.
card.stand_here: Go to the phone icon on the map, then walk to the terrace at the back and side of the church and face the city. Confirm the exact spot when you arrive.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big city view from the terrace. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the two towers and Piazza Maggiore in the distance. Save zoom 0.5x for the basilica from the forecourt, so the facade and dome fit in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the city and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunset is the time most guides recommend for the city view. Late afternoon gives warm light on the basilica's facade.
card.selfie_here: Try the courtyard in front of the basilica, with the sanctuary behind you, ideally in the golden hour before sunset. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm up a bit so the dome fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At Porta Saragozza, where the portico starts, ask someone to photograph you with the arches climbing away behind you (the sanctuary may not fit in the frame).
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are allowed inside, but skip them during Mass or services. The interior may be restricted or closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go. Bring water, especially on warm days, because the portico climb is long.
card.challenge: Find an arch around the terrace and use it as a picture frame for the city. Bonus points if the rooftops stay in the lower half and your horizon stays dead level.
card.good_to_know: The present church dates from 1723 and was designed by Carlo Francesco Dotti. The covered portico up the hill has 666 arches and runs for 3.8 km, built between 1674 and 1793. It's part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Porticoes of Bologna.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the phone icon on the map, then walk to the terrace at the back and side of the church and face the city. Confirm the exact spot when you arrive.

card.hook: Neptune has his left arm stretched out like he's calming the waves, and on a busy day he looks like he's calming the crowd too. He's tall, dark and clearly outlined, so he looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno, on the Piazza Maggiore side of the basin, and face Neptune so the big bulk of the Basilica di San Petronio fills the space behind him. That's the shot that says 'Bologna'.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic Neptune-and-basilica framing. Try 0.5x to fit the whole basin and the water jets, but keep the statue away from the edges so he doesn't look stretched. Zoom 2x to 5x is great for his face, trident and outstretched hand (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the dark bronze keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Go before about 9 a.m., when the square is nearly empty, or just after sunrise. In the evening the lit tower of Palazzo d'Accursio makes a lovely backdrop, so switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out in front of you. Turn so Neptune and the basin are over your shoulder, and keep your arm steady so he doesn't get cut off.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the square, toward Via Ugo Bassi, while you stand near the basin, and ask them to get the whole fountain in, not just the statue. In the evening they'll catch Neptune against the floodlit tower of Palazzo d'Accursio.
card.rules_and_safety: Early service vehicles and cleaning machines cross the square, so keep an eye out and stay out of the main flow of walkers.
card.challenge: Find the spot where Neptune's outstretched thumb lines up with his body for the 'stone of shame' joke: crouch low, shoot from the stone, and see if your friends get it.
card.good_to_know: The fountain was designed by Tommaso Laureti and finished in 1565, and Giambologna's bronze Neptune was fixed in place around 1566. Cardinal Legate Charles Borromeo commissioned it to celebrate his uncle's election as Pope Pius IV. It was restored in 2016-2017, so older photos show a darker, greener bronze.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno, on the Piazza Maggiore side of the basin, and face Neptune so the big bulk of the Basilica di San Petronio fills the space behind him. That's the shot that says 'Bologna'.

ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the far side of the square, nearer Via Ugo Bassi. From there you get him against the tower of Palazzo d'Accursio, which is better in the evening once the floodlights come on. The source describes this as a shot of the statue, not explicitly of the whole fountain, so the photographer should check the framing includes the basin.

sources.title: Fontana del Nettuno: Bologna's Neptune Statue & Fountain

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the fountain behind them for a selfie, so I left selfie_spots empty rather than guess. The closest named spot is the 'stone of shame' (pietra della vergogna) in front of the Salaborsa library: <cite index="7-4">stand on the dark paving stone set into the ground in front of Biblioteca Salaborsa and look up at Neptune.</cite> That puts the statue in front of the visitor, the opposite of what you asked for, and sources disagree on its exact position: one says <cite index="9-6">walk round behind the statue, to the foot of the entrance steps of the Salaborsa library</cite>. For the ask-someone spot, the 'Piazza Maggiore side' shot is described as <cite index="15-7">Neptune with the bulk of the basilica behind him</cite>, which is a statue shot rather than a visitor shot. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules. The only crowd-related remark is that <cite index="17-16">there's no admission fee or barriers, which means constant crowds and people climbing on it despite cameras everywhere.</cite>, which I did not treat as a safety point.

card.hook: Picture one arch, then 665 more just like it, all marching uphill towards a church. That's the Portico of San Luca, and it's a gift if you like a photo that looks like a pattern.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Arco del Meloncello, on the lower part of the climb. Face south-west and look up the covered walkway as it climbs towards the sanctuary.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the arch and the portico climbing away from it. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to squeeze the arches together into a stack going up the hill. Use 0.5x only if you want the arch to fill the frame, and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the middle of the walkway on the centre line, then tap the far arches and slide the brightness down a touch so the bright opening at the far end doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually the softest light and the quietest time. The climb is long, so give yourself plenty of time and check the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Try the Arco del Meloncello, right under the arch where the portico crosses the road. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the arcade running up the hill behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the road side of the arch, while you stand on the Arco del Meloncello bridge with the covered walkway climbing the hill behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Avoid midday in summer on the uphill walk, because the heat can be punishing and parts of the portico don't give full shade. Bring sunscreen, a hat and water. For the church, the dome and any paid terrace, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap and catch exactly one walker in the arches, so your photo shows just how long this thing is.
card.good_to_know: The portico has 666 arches and is about 3.8 km long. It was built between 1674 and 1793 to shelter the yearly procession carrying the icon of the Virgin Mary between the sanctuary and the cathedral. It's widely described as the longest portico in the world, and it joined the UNESCO listing for the Porticoes of Bologna in 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Arco del Meloncello, on the lower part of the climb. Face south-west and look up the covered walkway as it climbs towards the sanctuary.

card.hook: Skip the queue of postcards for a second: this calm, dignified façade on a University-district street is a great photo before you even step inside.
card.stand_here: Follow the phone icon to via delle Belle Arti 56, because the building is right there. Face the front and step back along the pavement as far as is safe to fit more of it in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole front. If the street is too tight, tap 0.5x, then try 2x (if your phone has it) for details higher up the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime is best, when the façade is evenly lit. On a bright day, early or late sun gives softer shadows on the walls.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold it a little higher than your face, and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it. Then turn so the building fills the space over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside change from room to room, so check the official site before you go and follow the signs and staff. Outside, only step back along the pavement as far as is safe.
card.challenge: Take three shots: the whole front, a doorway, then a window. Which one would you frame on your wall?
card.good_to_know: This is Bologna's national art gallery, in a former Jesuit novitiate called the Saint Ignatius building. Alfonso Torreggiani designed it in 1726, and the Academy of Fine Arts shares it. Inside you'll find Emilian painting from the 13th to the 18th century, including Guido Reni's Massacre of the Innocents.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Follow the phone icon to via delle Belle Arti 56, because the building is right there. Face the front and step back along the pavement as far as is safe to fit more of it in.

selfie_research.notes: No fetched page names a selfie spot with the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna behind the visitor, or a passer-by spot for a photo of the visitor with the whole building. The results were general photo-spot lists, museum pages, Wikimedia Commons files and address pages. The Wanderlog 'best photo spots' list includes the museum but gives no framing advice. Wikimedia Commons shows porticoes on Via delle Belle Arti, but no page calls them a selfie or photo spot, so I left them out. No page states any selfie stick or tripod rule. One travel blog (tastebologna.net, 'Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna: what to see, hours & tickets') says non-flash photography is allowed inside. That is not a selfie-stick rule, so it is not listed under rules. The museum is at Via delle Belle Arti 56, 40126 Bologna. Please check the spots on the ground before adding them to the app.

card.hook: Somewhere on these walls is a painted crest for a student you've never heard of, and there are about six thousand to choose from. Start with the long row of arches, then let yourself get nosy.
card.stand_here: Stand under the portico of the Archiginnasio, right at the phone icon on the map, and face along the line of arches so they run away from you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole run of arches in. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the columns, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single coat of arms or bust.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the arches don't lean, then tap the brightest part of the wall and slide it a touch darker to keep the colours of the painted arms.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime so you can see the painted coats of arms clearly under the portico. Early morning or a softly overcast day usually means fewer people and gentler light on the arches.
card.selfie_here: Head into the inner courtyard (Il Cortile) and stand under the arcades with the painted coats of arms on the walls behind you. The covered space gives soft, even light, so use the front camera and hold it a little low to fit the crests over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Piazza Galvani, where the building's address is (Piazza Galvani 1), to frame you with the whole facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash is allowed anywhere in the Archiginnasio, because the wooden carvings are fragile. In the library reading room, photos are only allowed from the entrance doorway, and photo rules in the Anatomical Theatre vary, so ask before you shoot. You'll also be asked to leave bags at the entrance.
card.challenge: Find one coat of arms or bust you'd happily call your favourite, fill the frame with it, then give it a name and a very dramatic backstory.
card.good_to_know: The Archiginnasio was the main building of the University of Bologna, and today it houses the city's municipal library. It went up fast, with work starting in February 1562 and the doors opening in October 1563. Upstairs, the Anatomical Theatre is a fir-wood amphitheatre from 1636 that was rebuilt after wartime bombing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand under the portico of the Archiginnasio, right at the phone icon on the map, and face along the line of arches so they run away from you.

selfie_spots.name: Archiginnasio inner courtyard (Il Cortile)

selfie_spots.why: The courtyard's walls and ceilings are covered in painted student crests, and the covered space gives soft, even light, which suits a close selfie.

card.hook: Picture a big city park where the whole show is a pond, with a curving water path leading your eye off to the far end of the lake. That's Giardini Margherita, and the lake is its best subject for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Chalet dei Giardini Margherita, on the lakeside terrace. Face out across the pond so the banks, the trees and the curving water path all sit in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full view across the pond. Go to 0.5x if you want more trees and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the far end of the lake.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water's edge on the lower line and let the path curve into the shot.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the water and fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto one of the little bridges across the central lake and turn so the water and the park are behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the scenery in.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public garden, but check the official site for any opening times or restrictions on the Chalet and its terrace.
card.challenge: Find a tree reflected in the water and see if you can fit its twin, upside down, into the bottom third of your photo.
card.good_to_know: The park opened on 6 July 1879, on land the city bought from an ancient convent. Ernesto Baldo Bertone di Sambuy designed it as an English landscape garden, which is why it feels relaxed rather than formal. In the main square, look for the liberty-style building that was an astronomical observatory for many years.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Chalet dei Giardini Margherita, on the lakeside terrace. Face out across the pond so the banks, the trees and the curving water path all sit in front of you.

card.hook: Bologna's town hall wears a terracotta clock tower like a very stylish hat, and the big open square in front of it gives you room to show it off. Step back, breathe out, and fit the whole thing in.
card.stand_here: Stand on the west side of Piazza Maggiore, near the Fontana del Nettuno. From there the palace is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west, so face north-west and you'll see the stone façade across the square.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole façade and clock tower in one shot, then try 1x for a more natural look. For the clock tower, coats of arms and the statue over the doorway, use 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap the façade and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Weekday mornings tend to be quieter. Late afternoon brings warm, golden light that suits the stone and terracotta.
card.selfie_here: Try the palace façade on the square near the Neptune Fountain, where the carved eagle reliefs make a detailed backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the palace wall over your shoulder. The shaded inner courtyard, with its arches framing you, is another option.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to shoot from the west side of Piazza Maggiore, where the palace fronts the square, while you stand with the façade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The courtyard is inside the palace, so check access on the official site before you go. Photo rules in some rooms may differ too.
card.challenge: Get a close-up of the terracotta Madonna and Child, then zoom to the bronze Pope Gregory XIII above the doorway. Two statues, one building, zero neck cramp if you use your zoom.
card.good_to_know: Palazzo d'Accursio began as the home of the jurist Accursius and grew by taking in neighbouring buildings. In 1336 it became the seat of the Anziani, the commune's senior magistrates, and Fioravante Fioravanti added the clock tower in the 15th century. Today it also holds the Civic Art Collection, the Museo Morandi and the Biblioteca Salaborsa.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the west side of Piazza Maggiore, near the Fontana del Nettuno. From there the palace is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west, so face north-west and you'll see the stone façade across the square.

card.hook: Bologna Cathedral is a big church on a narrow street, and you can't step back far enough to fit it all in. Good news: that squeeze is what gives you strong vertical lines, carved stone and deep shadows under the arches.
card.stand_here: Stand on Via dell'Indipendenza, under the porticoes on the cathedral side of the street, facing the Baroque façade. From there the cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot from its doors. Check the exact spot under the arches when you arrive.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in as much of the front as the street allows. Then try 1x for a calmer view of the middle part, and zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the upper windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the façade's vertical edges up with them and hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the building lean.
card.best_time: Try the afternoon and early evening, when the sun is likely to reach the front.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the cathedral rise behind you over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little low and tilt it up slightly to catch more of the tall front.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the pavement right in front of the Baroque façade and ask a passer-by to shoot upward at zoom 0.5x, since the front is hard to fit from farther back.
card.rules_and_safety: The street and its porticoes are public, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site for visiting arrangements and dress code before you go in.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a portico arch framing the edge, then one deliberately close crop of the carved stone, and pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: This is the Metropolitan Cathedral of Saint Peter, the seat of the city's archbishop. A cathedral has stood here since at least 1028, and most of what you see today dates from the 17th century. The Baroque façade was added between 1743 and 1747 by Alfonso Torreggiani, on the instructions of Pope Benedict XIV. The round-based bell tower is the second tallest in Bologna after the Asinelli Tower.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Via dell'Indipendenza, under the porticoes on the cathedral side of the street, facing the Baroque façade. From there the cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot from its doors. Check the exact spot under the arches when you arrive.

card.hook: Porta Saragozza looks like it was built to stop an army, and the best part is that the whole red-brick gate, both towers and the castle-style battlements, fits in one frame. Bring your sense of drama.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza di Porta Saragozza, in front of the gate on the city-side approach, and face the gate so it sits straight ahead of you. Leave a little sky above and a little square around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get both towers and the arch between them. If you're close and the towers get cut off, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the battlements and brick detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the brick and fewer people in the square. At midday the sun is behind the gate, so tap the brickwork and nudge it brighter.
card.selfie_here: Walk under the arcade on Via Saragozza, the stretch that ends at the gate, around sunset, when the light is gorgeous. Or step under one of the two smaller pedestrian arches beside the central one. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the gate or the arches over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the pavement outside the gate, facing it, with the Bonaccorsi arch alongside and the start of the Portico di San Luca across the road, while you pose with the gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the towers or any viewing area isn't confirmed, so check the official site before you go. Traffic and passers-by can wander into your shot.
card.challenge: Take your best 'I'm defending the city' pose in front of the battlements, then turn around and shoot the view back through the arch toward town.
card.good_to_know: The gate was built into Bologna's medieval walls in the 13th and 14th centuries, and by 1334 it had a drawbridge over a moat. In 1674 the long Portico di San Luca was built to link the city to the Basilica of San Luca, and the gate became the start of the yearly procession carrying the sacred icon. That's why it was also called the Porta Sacra or Porta dei Pellegrini. Its castle-like look dates from 1859, when architect Giuseppe Mengoli joined two crenellated arches to the round towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza di Porta Saragozza, in front of the gate on the city-side approach, and face the gate so it sits straight ahead of you. Leave a little sky above and a little square around it.

card.hook: Picture a square shaped like a slice of pizza, with a brick church sitting at the pointy end. That's Piazza Santo Stefano, and guides often call it the most photogenic square in Bologna.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Santo Stefano at the wide end of the wedge and face east. The basilica is only a short step away, so this photo takes about a minute.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which shows the church with the palazzi on each side much as your eye sees it. If the square feels cramped, try 0.5x to squeeze in more porticoes, but keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean. For brick details, 2x to 5x works, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the church on the centre line, with the portico edges running in from both sides.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the low sun crosses the square and there are fewer people. Late afternoon or evening gives golden light too, but the square gets busier then.
card.selfie_here: Stand under the porticoes along the side of the piazza with the church behind you, so the arches frame you. Use the front camera and try 0.5x if your phone has it. For a closer portrait, the narrow lane near Via Clavature 8 gives you the Santo Stefano complex as an old-stone backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the wide end of the piazza on the Via Santo Stefano side and shoot back toward the basilica, while you stand nearer the church so the whole building fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography in the public square is generally allowed. Inside the churches, look for signs first, because flash or filming may be prohibited, and check the official site for the courtyard and church rules.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and try to get the whole wedge of the square with the church dead centre. Bonus points if the square looks like it belongs only to you.
card.good_to_know: Santo Stefano isn't one church but a cluster of linked buildings that Bolognese people call the Sette Chiese, or Seven Churches. Tradition says Saint Petronius, a 5th-century bishop, founded it on the site of a temple of Isis, to recall the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. The oldest parts date to the 4th and 5th centuries, and the Courtyard of Pilate inside is 13th-century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Santo Stefano at the wide end of the wedge and face east. The basilica is only a short step away, so this photo takes about a minute.

card.hook: Neptune is standing right in front of a 13th-century brick palace, and somehow he isn't the one in charge of the view. Palazzo Re Enzo's battlements and plain brick walls are the star here, and your phone will love them.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno on the west side, facing the palace's entrance and the Neptune Fountain. Let the fountain fill the bottom of your screen with the brick façade rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the fountain and the palace front look natural together. If the façade won't fit, tap 0.5x, and try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the battlements and brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain low in the frame and keep your phone level so the tall brick walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Afternoon or early evening is worth a try, when the brick may glow with warmer light. Go early in the morning if you'd like fewer people in the square.
card.selfie_here: Stay in Piazza del Nettuno, in the open square near the Fountain of Neptune, with the palace's brick façade behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it) and let the palace rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on Via Rizzoli, near the corner with the Lampione dei Neonati lantern, while you stand in Piazza Re Enzo with the palace behind you, and ask them to frame the palace from the side.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the palace isn't covered in scaffolding before you go, as restoration work can spoil the view. Inside is open only for events and exhibitions, so check the official site if you want to go in.
card.challenge: Can you get Neptune, the battlements and your own grin in one shot without anyone's head sneaking in front of the fountain?
card.good_to_know: The palace was built between 1244 and 1246 as an extension of the Podestà building, which had become too small for the city's government. It's named after Enzio of Sardinia, son of Emperor Frederick II, who was held here as a prisoner from 1249 until he died in 1272. Much of its Gothic look comes from a 1905 restoration by Alfonso Rubbiani, so you're seeing a carefully revived medieval style.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno on the west side, facing the palace's entrance and the Neptune Fountain. Let the fountain fill the bottom of your screen with the brick façade rising behind it.

card.hook: The ground here is paved in little pebbles, just like it was in medieval times, so your first photo might be of your own feet. Look up and you get a Romanesque facade with a big round rose window staring back at you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza San Domenico, where the basilica is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east. Face south-east so the facade and rose window fill your screen, with a statue or tomb from the square low in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and a statue or tomb in front of it. Switch to 1x for a tidier view. Then try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to home in on the rose window and the Madonna statue.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the picture a little darker so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when the light falls on the facade and the Madonna statue.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the column of Saint Dominic in the square, with the statue on its pillar next to you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low, so the church should stay behind your shoulder. For a second go, stand beside the raised tomb of Rolandino de' Passeggeri, which also puts the facade behind you.
card.ask_someone: After you've looked at the tombs, ask someone to cross the road and face back toward the church, then pose by the tomb so they get the whole facade with you in front. The exact spot is loose, so just step back until the whole front fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the basilica is generally allowed but usually without flash. Check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules.
card.challenge: Get a statue or tomb low in the frame and the rose window high up, with the building standing straight against the gridlines. Bonus points if your feet and the pebbles sneak in.
card.good_to_know: The facade dates from 1240 and was restored in 1910. The column with the Madonna of the Rosary (1632) was put up after a design by Guido Reni to mark the end of a plague. Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominicans, died in the church on 6 August 1221, and his shrine inside was worked on by several artists, including the young Michelangelo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza San Domenico, where the basilica is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east. Face south-east so the facade and rose window fill your screen, with a statue or tomb from the square low in front of you.

card.hook: Here's the surprise: this huge civic palazzo has two lanes of shops running right through its ground floor. Step back across the open square and the whole brick-and-sandstone front fits in one frame, tower and all.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Maggiore, in the historic centre of Bologna, facing the palazzo's facade. The palazzo is directly north of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Basilica di San Petronio will be close by in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the wide view of the facade and tower across the square. If you can't squeeze the whole front in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or more for the arches, statues and brick and sandstone textures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the facade, then slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the sandstone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Golden hour is lovely here, because the warm light suits the sandstone. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try the Voltone del Podestà, the arcade under the palazzo on the Piazza Maggiore side. Stand under the arches with the square open behind you, use the front camera (0.5x if you want more in), and let the busy square be your backdrop. It's the best fit we could find, so see how it looks when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of Piazza Maggiore while you stand in front of the facade, and suggest 0.5x so the palazzo and its portico fit in next to San Petronio.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the palazzo are allowed for personal use, but the interior may only be open during exhibitions. Flash is typically not allowed in the Salone della Podestà, so check the signs at the entrance.
card.challenge: Find one of the terracotta statues under the arcade and frame it so it looks like it's watching the square.
card.good_to_know: The Palazzo del Podestà was built around 1200 as the seat of the podestà, the commune's officials. In 1245 the Palazzo Re Enzo was added beside it, topped by the Torre dell'Arengo, whose bell called people together in emergencies. In 1453 Aristotile Fioravanti rebuilt the old Gothic facade in Renaissance style for Giovanni II Bentivoglio.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Maggiore, in the historic centre of Bologna, facing the palazzo's facade. The palazzo is directly north of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Basilica di San Petronio will be close by in the frame.

card.hook: Step into Piazza Rossini and the whole front of San Giacomo Maggiore is right there, pointed windows and all, like it's posing for you. Your only job is to stand still and not let the walls lean.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Rossini, in front of the main facade, and face the church. The church lies to the north-east of it, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the head-on view. If the square feels tight, tap 0.5x to fit the whole front plus some sky. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the pointed windows and the little statue niche at the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up a vertical edge of the facade with a grid line, then tap the pale stonework and drag the brightness slider down a little so the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive. Early in the day is usually calmer on the square.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Piazza Rossini, facing the church front, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold your phone level so the facade sits over your shoulder. It's our best guess for the spot, so have a play with the angle.
card.ask_someone: For a shot of you with the church and bell tower together, ask someone to take it from Piazza Verdi, the square behind the church, where both fit in nicely.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the church is banned, so keep your photos to the outside. Visiting hours and access may change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the small statue niche near the top of the facade and zoom in on it without letting the walls tilt.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1267, the church was finished in 1315 and it was consecrated in 1344. The facade is the oldest part, with tall pointed windows framed in pale Istrian stone, added in 1295. The brick bell tower came in 1471, and the Bentivoglio family added the long portico in 1477–1481.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Rossini, in front of the main facade, and face the church. The church lies to the north-east of it, about 1 minute on foot.
